nodes.statement: Radical novelty must be defined precisely before its consequences can be pursued.
nodes.span: we have to be much more precise as to what we mean in this context by the adjective "radical"
nodes.status_reason: follows from the reader's ordinary logical requirement that a key term be defined

nodes.statement: People habitually plan for the future using concepts inherited from past experience.
nodes.span: The usual way in which we plan today for tomorrow is in yesterday's vocabulary.
nodes.status_reason: an observation the reader can check but which is not derived from anything prior

nodes.statement: Linguists observe that word meanings evolve only slowly and gradually.
nodes.span: the meanings of words evolve over time, but also know that this is a slow and gradual process
nodes.status_reason: cited observation, checkable but not derived

nodes.statement: Coping with novelty by metaphor and analogy works under slow change but breaks down at a sharp discontinuity.
nodes.span: Under sufficiently slow and gradual change, it works reasonably well; in the case of a sharp discontinuity, however, the method breaks down
nodes.status_reason: follows from n2 and n3 given that past experience must resemble the new case for analogy to hold

nodes.statement: A radical novelty is precisely the case where past experience is irrelevant and metaphors mislead.
nodes.span: This is the situation that is characteristic for the "radical" novelty.
nodes.status_reason: definitional consequence of n4, satisfying the demand in n1

nodes.statement: Radical novelty requires an orthogonal method: approaching it with a blank mind, refusing links to the familiar.
nodes.span: Coping with radical novelty requires an orthogonal method.
nodes.status_reason: derived from n5 since the familiar is stipulated inadequate

nodes.statement: Grasping a radical novelty is like learning a foreign language untranslatable into one's mother tongue.
nodes.span:
amounts to creating and learning a new foreign language that can 
not
 be translated into one's mother tongue
nodes.status_reason: an illustrative restatement of n6 whose warrant rests on quantum mechanics, not held by the reader

nodes.statement: Because adjusting to radical novelties is hard work, they are unwelcome and tend to be suppressed or denied.
nodes.span: radical novelties are so disturbing that they tend to be suppressed or ignored
nodes.status_reason: derived from n6's demand for hard work plus the stated unpopularity

nodes.statement: Gauss suppressed his discovery of non-Euclidean geometry out of fear, leaving others to take the criticism.
nodes.span: when he decided to suppress his discovery of non-Euclidean geometry, thus leaving it to Bolyai and Lobatchewsky to receive the flak
nodes.status_reason: historical citation offered as evidence, not derived

nodes.statement: The Middle Ages combined rampant reasoning by analogy with near-total intellectual stagnation.
nodes.span: "reasoning by analogy" was rampant; another characteristic was almost total intellectual stagnation
nodes.status_reason: historical claim asserted as evidence

nodes.statement: Reasoning by analogy and intellectual stagnation go together, so unwarranted analogies mark medieval thinking today.
nodes.span: and we now see why the two go together
nodes.status_reason: drawn from n4/n5 together with the historical pairing in n10

nodes.statement: A very large fraction of the population treats gradual change as the only paradigm of history.
nodes.span: the fraction of the population for which gradual change seems to be all but the only paradigm of history is very large
nodes.status_reason: supported only by the author's personal observation

nodes.statement: The mathematical community tacitly assumes mathematical activity will remain essentially unchanged.
nodes.span: the vast majority of the mathematical community has never challenged its tacit assumption that doing mathematics will remain very much the same
nodes.status_reason: asserted example supporting n12

nodes.statement: Robbins argues no quantum leap in mathematical ability is possible because the human mind is unchanged.
nodes.span: The human mind is no different now from what it was five thousand years ago.
nodes.status_reason: quoted testimony, checkable as quoted

nodes.statement: Robbins evades radical novelty by defining mathematics as whatever it has always been, rather than admitting alternatives to brain usage.
nodes.span: thus exorcizing the danger of radical novelty by the simple device of adjusting his definitions to his needs
nodes.status_reason: derived from n14 by the author's counter-analogy about faster alternatives to running

nodes.statement: Prevailing educational practice takes imperceptible gradual change as its exclusive paradigm, disguising novelty as familiar.
nodes.span: It is the prevailing educational practice, for which gradual, almost imperceptible, change seems to be the exclusive paradigm.
nodes.status_reason: illustrated by examples but not derived

nodes.statement: Arithmetic teaching disguises 'plus' as 'and' and restricts examples to visible familiar objects; calculus courses are tailored per major.
nodes.span: the hideous arithmetic operator "plus" is carefully disguised by calling it "and"
nodes.status_reason: concrete instances supporting n16

nodes.statement: Failing to prepare the next generation for radical novelties is a serious educational shortcoming.
nodes.span: I consider the failure of an educational practice to prepare the next generation for the phenomenon of radical novelties a serious shortcoming
nodes.status_reason: follows from n6 and n16, with the Cervera anecdote offered as justification of 'serious'

nodes.statement: The Cervera Rector's rejection of 'the dangerous novelty of thinking' and Spain's later troubles illustrate the cost.
nodes.span: Far be from us, Sire, the dangerous novelty of thinking
nodes.status_reason: anecdote adduced in support of n18

nodes.statement: Radical novelties matter now because science and technology keep inflicting them while we remain ill-prepared.
nodes.span: while we are ill-prepared to cope with them, science and technology have now shown themselves expert at inflicting them upon us
nodes.status_reason: combines n8/n12 with the cited scientific and technological examples

nodes.statement: Automatic computers constitute a radical novelty, and identifying them as such is required to expose surrounding nonsense.
nodes.span: automatic computers represent a radical novelty and that only by identifying them as such can we identify all the nonsense
nodes.status_reason: the central contention, announced before its supporting arguments are given

nodes.statement: Computers embody not one but two radical novelties.
nodes.span: automatic computers embody not only one radical novelty but two of them
nodes.status_reason: derived from n23 and n29 taken together

nodes.statement: The first radical novelty follows from raw computing power: programming demands conceptual hierarchies far deeper than any before.
nodes.span: The first radical novelty is a direct consequence of the raw power of today's computing equipment.
nodes.status_reason: derived from the divide-and-rule method n24 plus the size-ratio argument n25/n26

nodes.statement: We cope with big complex things by hierarchical decomposition into parts, repeated as needed.
nodes.span: divide and rule, i.e. we view the whole as a compositum of parts and deal with the parts separately
nodes.status_reason: familiar method asserted with everyday examples, not derived

nodes.statement: The depth of a hierarchical decomposition is roughly the logarithm of the size ratio between whole and smallest part.
nodes.span: the depth of a hierarchical decomposition is some sort of logarithm of the ratio of the "sizes"
nodes.status_reason: a quantitative rule stated without derivation and not available to a reader holding no formal apparatus

nodes.statement: Computing spans a size ratio from a bit to hundreds of megabytes and a microsecond to half an hour, a baffling ratio.
nodes.span: From a bit to a few hundred megabytes, from a microsecond to a half an hour of computing
nodes.status_reason: stated magnitudes the reader can check against ordinary units

nodes.statement: Programming is the only discipline in which such a gigantic ratio must be bridged by a single technology, exceeding even mathematical theories in depth.
nodes.span: his is the only discipline and profession in which such a gigantic ratio, which totally baffles our imagination, has to be bridged by a single technology
nodes.status_reason: derived from n24-n26

nodes.statement: Believers in gradual change cannot see this novelty and liken a computer to a bigger cash register, an absurdly shallow analogy.
nodes.span: For him, an automatic computer is something like the familiar cash register, only somewhat bigger, faster, and more flexible.
nodes.status_reason: instance of n8/n12 applied to n23

nodes.statement: The second radical novelty is that the computer is our first large-scale digital device.
nodes.span: The second radical novelty is that the automatic computer is our first large-scale digital device.
nodes.status_reason: derived from n30-n32 contrasting discrete with analogue mechanisms

nodes.statement: Almost all familiar mechanisms are treated as analogue, their behaviour a continuous function of parameters.
nodes.span: the vast majority of our mechanisms are viewed as analogue devices whose behaviour is over a large range a continuous function
nodes.status_reason: asserted with pencil and violin examples

nodes.statement: We also view ourselves as analogue devices, expecting more effort to give better results.
nodes.span: we view ourselves primarily as analogue devices: if we push a little harder we expect to do a little better
nodes.status_reason: assertion illustrated but not derived

nodes.statement: Assumed monotonicity licenses testing only the extremes, as with a hammer on the smallest and largest nails.
nodes.span: we try it out on the smallest and largest nails of the range, and if the outcomes of those two experiments are positive
nodes.status_reason: everyday example, checkable, supports n30

nodes.statement: Viewing a program as a familiar mechanism is dangerous because a single-bit change can have drastic consequences.
nodes.span: the smallest possible perturbations —i.e. changes of a single bit— can have the most drastic consequences
nodes.status_reason: derived from n29 contrasted with the continuity assumptions n30-n32

nodes.statement: Redundancy or error correction does not essentially alter this picture.
nodes.span: the picture is not essentially changed by the introduction of redundancy or error correction
nodes.status_reason: asserted as a scope caveat without argument

nodes.statement: In computing there is and will be no meaningful metric in which small changes produce small effects.
nodes.span: there is no meaningful metric in which "small" changes and "small" effects go hand in hand, and there never will be
nodes.status_reason: a strong universal claim asserted beyond what n33 establishes

nodes.statement: The second novelty is denied because admitting it would be discomforting, at enormous cost.
nodes.span: it is denied, because its truth would be too discomforting
nodes.status_reason: instance of the suppression pattern n8

nodes.statement: Evidence for radicality will be supplied by explaining strange phenomena as efforts at hiding the unfamiliar.
nodes.span: I shall do so by explaining a number of otherwise strange phenomena as frantic
nodes.status_reason: the argumentative strategy licensed by n8: denial predicts observable symptoms

nodes.statement: Software engineering is a doomed discipline because its charter, 'how to program if you cannot', is self-contradictory.
nodes.span: software engineering has accepted as its charter "How to program if you cannot."
nodes.status_reason: asserted from reading its literature; the self-contradiction is claimed rather than shown

nodes.statement: A US manufacturer created hundreds of 'software engineers' overnight by renaming its programmers.
nodes.span: it hired, one night, hundreds of new "software engineers" by the simple device of elevating all its programmers
nodes.status_reason: anecdote offered as evidence that the name is merely symbolic

nodes.statement: Measuring programmer productivity in lines of code produced follows from the illusion that programs are ordinary devices; lines should be booked as spent, not produced.
nodes.span: we should not regard them as "lines produced" but as "lines spent"
nodes.status_reason: derived from n33: programs are not devices, so device-style output metrics misbook the count

nodes.statement: Testing can demonstrate the presence of bugs but never their absence, yet software engineers keep refining testing.
nodes.span: program testing may convincingly demonstrate the presence of bugs, but can never demonstrate their absence
nodes.status_reason: a well-publicized remark quoted, not derived here

nodes.statement: Device-based quality control is misapplied to programs, as the persistence of testing strategies shows.
nodes.span: also that of quality control continues to be distorted by the reassuring illusion that what works with other devices works with programs as well
nodes.status_reason: derived from n33 plus the testing limitation n41

nodes.statement: The term 'software maintenance' leads people to believe programs wear out, as in the oil company blaming PASCAL.
nodes.span: its PASCAL programs did not last as long as its FORTRAN programs "because PASCAL was not maintained"
nodes.status_reason: anecdote supporting the mechanism-analogy diagnosis

nodes.statement: Attributing software difficulties to missing 'programming tools' rests on a shallow analogy worthy of the Middle Ages.
nodes.span: the shallowness of the underlying analogy is worthy of the Middle Ages
nodes.status_reason: applies the analogy critique n11 to the tools claim

nodes.statement: Artificial Intelligence is popular because a computer simulating a familiar noncomputer is less frightening.
nodes.span: the frightening computer becomes less frightening if it is used only to simulate a familiar noncomputer
nodes.status_reason: an instance of the flight-to-the-familiar pattern n4-n8, though acknowledged as controversial

nodes.statement: All computers can do is manipulate symbols and produce results of such manipulations, in a discrete world of unimaginable scale.
nodes.span: the only thing computers can do for us is to manipulate symbols and produce results of such manipulations
nodes.status_reason: rests on the discreteness and magnitude points n26, n29

nodes.statement: A program is best described as an abstract symbol manipulator made concrete by supplying a computer.
nodes.span: the program is an abstract symbol manipulator, which can be turned into a concrete one by supplying a computer to it
nodes.status_reason: a reformulation drawn from n46 plus the general-purpose/special-purpose account

nodes.statement: It helps to view a program as an elaborate formula in a formal system, making the programmer's task the derivation of that formula.
nodes.span: It really helps to view a program as a formula.
nodes.status_reason: proposed as a fruitful viewpoint whose warrant is its stated benefits, and formal systems are not held by the reader

nodes.statement: Mathematics ignored programming because programs were far longer formulae than it was used to.
nodes.span: programs were so much longer formulae than it was used to that it did not even recognize them as such
nodes.status_reason: offered as a consequence of n48

nodes.statement: The only reliable way to derive a program is by symbol manipulation, so mechanical symbol manipulators are built by human symbol manipulation.
nodes.span: We know of only one reliable way of doing that, viz. by means of symbol manipulation.
nodes.status_reason: the exclusivity claim is asserted, not argued

nodes.statement: Computing science is the interplay between mechanized and human symbol manipulation.
nodes.span: computing science is —and will always be— concerned with the interplay between mechanized and human symbol manipulation
nodes.status_reason: derived from n47 and n50

nodes.statement: On this definition 'automatic programming' is a contradiction in terms.
nodes.span: it reveals "automatic programming" as a contradiction in terms
nodes.status_reason: follows from n51 where programming is by definition the human half

nodes.statement: Computing science belongs near formal mathematics and applied logic, but aims at effective use of formal methods on a far larger scale.
nodes.span: in the direction of formal mathematics and applied logic, but ultimately far beyond where those are now
nodes.status_reason: located by n51

nodes.statement: In the long run computing science will realize part of Leibniz's Dream of symbolic calculation as an alternative to human reasoning.
nodes.span: realizing a significant part of Leibniz's Dream of providing symbolic calculation as an alternative to human reasoning
nodes.status_reason: a forecast resting on a named dream not held by the reader

nodes.statement: This vision meets widespread opposition from mathematicians, business, compulsive programmers, engineers, the military, soft sciences and educators.
nodes.span: it has met widespread —and sometimes even violent— opposition from all sorts of directions
nodes.status_reason: predicted by the denial-of-novelty pattern n8 and listed with instances

nodes.statement: Educational policy is determined not by scientific considerations but by extra-scientific expectations.
nodes.span: it is hardly influenced by scientific considerations derived from the topics taught, and almost entirely determined by extra-scientific circumstances
nodes.status_reason: asserted diagnosis, illustrated by rhetorical questions

nodes.statement: Flaherty reports that Canada's business elite dismisses academics as irrelevant and powerless.
nodes.span: the business elite dismisses traditional academics and intellectuals as largely irrelevant and powerless
nodes.status_reason: quoted source used to illustrate doubts about academic rhetoric

nodes.statement: The likely future of computing science education is 'business as usual': hard science avoided and curricula progressively infantilized.
nodes.span: The universities will continue to lack the courage to teach hard science
nodes.status_reason: projected from n55-n57

nodes.statement: Calling errors 'errors' rather than 'bugs' is more honest and changes an 'almost correct' program into a wrong one.
nodes.span: begin with cleaning up our language by no longer calling a bug a bug but by calling it an error
nodes.status_reason: follows from the rejection of animistic metaphor and from n35's denial of a small-effects metric

nodes.statement: Anthropomorphic terminology for programs and equipment should never be used or permitted.
nodes.span:
never
 refer to parts of programs or pieces of equipment in an anthropomorphic terminology
nodes.status_reason: derived from n61-n63 on why the personification is misleading and paralyzing

nodes.statement: Anthropomorphic metaphor has caused avoidable confusion wherever adopted and is a shallow analogy.
nodes.span: The analogy that underlies this personification is so shallow that it is not only misleading but also paralyzing.
nodes.status_reason: instance of the shallow-analogy critique n5/n11, supported by the author's encounters

nodes.statement: It is misleading because it treats the unfamiliar discrete in terms of the familiar continuous, namely ourselves.
nodes.span: it suggests that we can adequately cope with the unfamiliar discrete in terms of the familiar continuous
nodes.status_reason: derived from n29-n33 plus n31

nodes.statement: It is paralyzing because persons act in time, forcing operational semantics and thinking in terms of computational behaviours.
nodes.span: its adoption effectively prevents a departure from operational semantics and thus forces people to think about programs in terms of computational behaviours
nodes.status_reason: derived from the temporality of persons; operational semantics is glossed for the reader in behavioural terms

nodes.statement: Operational reasoning is a tremendous waste of mental effort.
nodes.span: operational reasoning is a tremendous waste of mental effort
nodes.status_reason: established later by the general principle n65 as applied in n71

nodes.statement: To demonstrate something about all elements of a large set, arguing from the set's definition is vastly more efficient than treating elements individually.
nodes.span:
if we have to demonstrate something about 
all
 the elements of a large set, it is hopelessly inefficient to deal with all the elements
nodes.status_reason: argued by the domino demonstration n66-n70

nodes.statement: The figure Q, an 8x8 square minus two opposite corner unit squares, has area 62, matching 31 dominos, yet cannot be covered by them.
nodes.span:
The theorem is that the figure 
Q
 cannot be covered by 31 of such dominos.
nodes.status_reason: proved by the colouring argument n68-n69

nodes.statement: One possible proof is to generate all placements of 31 dominos and check none yields Q, a tremendously laborious job.
nodes.span: a possible way of proving the theorem is by generating all possible placements of dominos and verifying for each placement
nodes.status_reason: a stated exhaustive procedure the reader can follow but which is not derived

nodes.statement: Colour the squares as a chess board; each domino covers one white and one black square, so any placement covers equal numbers.
nodes.span: Each domino, covering two adjacent squares, covers 1 white and 1 black square
nodes.status_reason: a self-contained construction checkable with ordinary counting

nodes.statement: In Q the counts of white and black squares differ by 2 because the removed corners lie on the same diagonal, so no placement yields Q.
nodes.span: the number of white squares and the number of black squares differ by 2 —opposite corners lying on the same diagonal
nodes.status_reason: derived from n68 by counting

nodes.statement: The colouring argument is not only far shorter but stronger, covering all even-sided rectangles, an infinite family the exhaustive method cannot handle.
nodes.span:
it covers the generalization of 
Q
 by replacing the original 8 by 8 square by 
any
 rectangle with sides of even length
nodes.status_reason: derived by comparing n67 with n68-n69 over an infinite family

nodes.statement: Since a program defines its set of possible computations, one should reason about the program text and ignore the computations.
nodes.span: deal with all computations possible under control of a given program by ignoring them and working with the program
nodes.status_reason: direct application of n65 to programs via the specification-as-universal-claim step

nodes.statement: A programming language with formal syntax and proof rules is a formal system for which execution is merely one model, and formal systems should be handled in their own right.
nodes.span: A programming language, with its formal syntax and with the proof rules that define its semantics, is a formal system for which program execution provides only a model.
nodes.status_reason: appeals to a 'well-known' fact about formal systems, an apparatus the reader does not hold

nodes.statement: Therefore we should reason about programs without mentioning their behaviours, and the anthropomorphic metaphor should be banned from computing science.
nodes.span: the corollary is that we should reason about programs without even mentioning their possible "behaviours"
nodes.status_reason: derived from n71, n72 together with n60 and n64

nodes.statement: A demonstrated educational program visualized features of computations, reinforcing exactly what students must unlearn.
nodes.span: they were used to display all sorts of features of computations evolving under control of the student's program
nodes.status_reason: reported observation used as a counterexample case

nodes.statement: Such systems will cause permanent mental damage because breaking bad habits is the hardest part of learning.
nodes.span: we must expect from that system permanent mental damage for most students exposed to it
nodes.status_reason: derived from n71/n73 plus the stated difficulty of unlearning

nodes.statement: A program alone is only half a conjecture; the other half is its functional specification, and the programmer must present the complete conjecture as a proven theorem.
nodes.span: a program is no more than half a conjecture. The other half of the conjecture is the functional specification
nodes.status_reason: derived from n48 and n71's specification-as-claim-about-all-computations

nodes.statement: An introductory course should teach predicate calculus as boolean algebra, renaming true/false as black/white to sever intuitive links.
nodes.span: we rename the values {true, false} of the boolean domain as {black, white}

nodes.statement: It should also teach a small clean imperative language whose semantics is defined by the proof rules accompanying each construct.
nodes.span: for whatever we introduce, the corresponding semantics is defined by the proof rules that go with it

nodes.statement: Students should be required to give a formal proof that the program meets its formal specification, designing proofs and programs together.
nodes.span: his main task is to give a formal proof that the program he proposes meets the equally formal functional specification
nodes.status_reason: derived from n76

nodes.statement: The language should be unimplemented on campus so students cannot be tempted to test their programs.
nodes.span: the programming language in question has not been implemented on campus so that students are protected from the temptation to test
nodes.status_reason: derived from n41 and n73: testing reinforces the banned operational view

nodes.statement: The objection that the author is out of touch with the real world fails, since real-world problems are those left after refusing effective solutions.
nodes.span: the problems of the real world are primarily those you are left with when you refuse to apply their effective solutions
nodes.status_reason: a rebuttal asserted by reframing rather than derived

nodes.statement: Since the early 1980s such a course has been given successfully to hundreds of freshmen each year.
nodes.span: since the early 80's, such an introductory programming course has successfully been given to hundreds of college freshmen each year
nodes.status_reason: empirical report refuting the too-difficult postulate; checkable as stated

nodes.statement: The objection that it is too difficult for freshmen is refuted by that experience.
nodes.span: that kite won't fly either for the postulate has been proven wrong
nodes.status_reason: derived from the evidence n82

nodes.statement: The objection that it would frustrate students fails because the few simple manipulation rules soon give students a sense of surpassing power.
nodes.span: the rules of manipulation are in this case so few and simple that very soon thereafter he makes the exciting discovery
nodes.status_reason: rests on the author's teaching experience rather than a derivation

nodes.statement: Teaching formal methods is rewarding: within months students gain a radically novel confidence and cultural dimension, which is what education is for.
nodes.span: within a few months, their concept of intellectual culture has acquired a radically novel dimension
nodes.status_reason: drawn from n84 and the course experience n82

nodes.statement: Universities should welcome teaching radical novelties, since this willingness is the main safeguard against dictatorships.
nodes.span: it is their calling to welcome the opportunity to do so
